title: Holiness unto the Lord
sections: The Lord can make me holy
Jesus Christ is the promised Messiah

sayings.text: The time is not come, the time that the LORD's house should be built.
sayings.speaker: The people, about the temple
sayings.why: The Lord, through Haggai, repeated what the people kept saying. About 15 years after coming home, they still had not rebuilt His house.

sayings.text: Who is left among you that saw this house in her first glory?
sayings.speaker: The Lord, through Haggai
sayings.why: Some old people remembered Solomon’s grand temple. The Lord asked them about it, then promised the new one greater glory (Haggai 2:9).

sayings.text: Turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will turn unto you
sayings.speaker: The Lord, through Zechariah
sayings.why: These were the Lord’s first words through Zechariah. When His people turn back to Him, He turns back to them.

sayings.text: Take away the filthy garments from him.
sayings.speaker: The angel, about Joshua
sayings.why: In Zechariah’s vision, the angel had Joshua’s dirty clothes taken off. Then he told Joshua, “I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee.”

sayings.text: Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit
sayings.speaker: The Lord, to Zerubbabel
sayings.why: An angel gave Zechariah this message for Zerubbabel, who had to finish the temple with few people and little money.

sayings.text: We will go with you: for we have heard that God is with you.
sayings.speaker: Many nations, to a Jew
sayings.why: Zechariah saw people from every language take hold of a Jew’s robe, wanting to come to the Lord with him.

sayings.text: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion
sayings.speaker: Zechariah, about the King
sayings.why: Zechariah told Jerusalem to rejoice because her King was coming, riding on a donkey. Jesus fulfilled it on Palm Sunday.

sayings.text: If ye think good, give me my price; and if not, forbear.
sayings.speaker: Zechariah, as a shepherd
sayings.why: Zechariah asked for his pay as a shepherd and got thirty pieces of silver. Judas later asked the priests, “What will ye give me” (Matthew 26:15).

sayings.text: What are these wounds in thine hands?
sayings.speaker: People, to the Lord
sayings.why: Zechariah foresaw this question. In Doctrine and Covenants 45:51 the Lord says the Jews will ask it when He comes again.

words.clue: earneth wages to put it into a bag with ____
words.mean: Working only for ourselves and leaving the Lord out is like putting our pay into a bag that leaks.

words.clue: and in this place will I give ____
words.mean: The Lord promised peace in His house. We can feel it in the temple today.

words.clue: he that toucheth you toucheth the ____ of his eye
words.mean: The Lord’s people are as precious to Him as the center of His own eye.

words.clue: I will clothe thee with change of ____
words.mean: Raiment means clothing. Through Jesus Christ, our sins can be taken away like dirty clothes.
Zechariah saw Jesus Christ, the King, coming humbly into Jerusalem on a donkey.

words.clue: So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of ____
words.mean: A shepherd was paid a tiny price. Judas sold Jesus for the same thirty pieces of silver.

words.clue: his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of ____
words.mean: When Jesus comes again, He will stand on the Mount of Olives to save His people.

deep.intro: The people felt their new temple was poor next to Solomon’s. Read what the Lord told them about His riches and the glory to come.
deep.q: In Haggai 2:8, what does the Lord say belongs to Him?
wrong: The stones of the old temple
deep.why: Verse 8: “The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the LORD of hosts.” He could give His house all it needed.
deep.find: The silver is mine, and the gold is mine
deep.hunt: In Haggai 2, what does the Lord say belongs to Him?

deep.intro: The lesson invites you to read what life will be like when the Lord dwells with His people. Picture Jerusalem as Zechariah saw it.
deep.q: In Zechariah 8:3, what will Jerusalem be called?
deep.why: Verse 3: “Jerusalem shall be called a city of truth; and the mountain of the LORD of hosts the holy mountain.”
deep.find: Jerusalem shall be called a city of truth
deep.hunt: In Zechariah 8, what will Jerusalem be called?

deep.intro: The lesson asks you to compare Zechariah 9:9 with the day Jesus came into Jerusalem. Read Matthew’s account of that day.
deep.q: In Matthew 21:3, what were the disciples to say if anyone asked why they took the donkeys?
deep.right: The Lord hath need of them
wrong: We will bring them back soon
The King will pay you well
deep.why: Verse 3: “The Lord hath need of them; and straightway he will send them.” Then Matthew says it fulfilled the prophet’s words (verse 4).
deep.find: The Lord hath need of them
deep.hunt: In Matthew 21, what were the disciples to say if anyone asked why they took the donkeys?

deep.title: From the children’s part of the lesson
deep.intro: The children’s part of this week’s lesson helps you picture Jesus riding into Jerusalem, and compare Zechariah’s prophecies with the New Testament.
deep.q: Which New Testament Stories chapter does the lesson suggest for Zechariah’s prophecy of the King on a donkey?
deep.why: It suggests The Savior Goes to Jerusalem, from New Testament Stories. Then children can point to the people in the pictures who are rejoicing.

deep.title: From For the Strength of Youth
deep.intro: This month’s For the Strength of Youth looks at Haggai’s call to consider your ways, and what it might sound like if he said it today.
deep.q: What modern question does the article say is like Haggai’s call to consider your ways?
deep.right: How’s that working out for you?
deep.why: The author says we might put it as asking how that’s working out for you. For the Israelites it was going poorly: they ate and drank but never felt full.
deep.find: How’s that working out for you?

reels.hook: Working hard, but the money leaks away.
reels.body: About 15 years after coming home from Babylon, the people had fine houses, but the Lord’s temple still lay in ruins (Haggai 1:4). So the Lord said, “Consider your ways” (Haggai 1:5). They planted a lot but harvested little. They ate but stayed hungry. Their pay seemed to drop into “a bag with holes.” Leaving the Lord out left them empty. His answer: get wood and build (Haggai 1:8).

verse.text: Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.

question.q: What did the Lord mean by “a bag with holes”?
question.right: Their work wasn’t filling their lives
wrong: They needed to sew better bags
question.why: They kept working, but it never filled them up, because they left the Lord’s house in ruins. So He said, “Consider your ways” (Haggai 1:7).

bonus.q: In Haggai 1:15, on what day did the people start working on the temple?
bonus.hunt: In Haggai 1, on what day did the people start working on the temple?
bonus.right: The 24th day of the sixth month
wrong: The first day of the seventh month
The tenth day of the first month
bonus.why: Verse 15: “In the four and twentieth day of the sixth month.” Haggai spoke on the first day of that month (verse 1), so they got to work 23 days later.
bonus.find: In the four and twentieth day of the sixth month

reels.hook: A plain little temple with a bigger future.
reels.body: Some old people had seen Solomon’s beautiful temple before it was destroyed. Next to it, the new one looked like nothing (Haggai 2:3). The Lord said, “Be strong … and work: for I am with you” (Haggai 2:4). He promised that “the desire of all nations shall come” (Haggai 2:7), a title for Jesus Christ. Centuries later, Jesus Himself taught in this temple. There, the Lord promised, He would give peace.

verse.text: The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts: and in this place will I give peace, saith the LORD of hosts.

question.q: Why would this plainer temple have the greater glory?
question.right: The Savior Himself would come to it
wrong: It would be covered in more gold
It would be twice as big as before
question.why: Haggai promised “the desire of all nations shall come” (Haggai 2:7) and fill the house with glory. Jesus Christ came and taught there.

bonus.q: In Haggai 2:5, the Lord reminds them of a covenant He made when they came out of where?
bonus.hunt: In Haggai 2, the Lord reminds them of a covenant He made when they came out of where?
bonus.why: Verse 5: “According to the word that I covenanted with you when ye came out of Egypt, so my spirit remaineth among you.” The God who freed Israel was with them still.
bonus.find: when ye came out of Egypt

image.alt: Painting of a plain, boxy stone temple with two tall pillars by its door, smoke rising from the altar beside it, and two men in robes walking across the courtyard

reels.hook: Big jobs get done God’s way, not by muscle.
reels.body: Zerubbabel had a huge job: finish the temple with few people and little money. An angel showed Zechariah a golden lampstand kept burning with olive oil. The message for Zerubbabel: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.” His problems looked like a mountain, but it would become flat ground (Zechariah 4:7). His hands began the temple, and “his hands shall also finish it” (Zechariah 4:9).

verse.text: Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.

question.q: How would Zerubbabel get the temple finished?
question.right: With help from the Lord’s Spirit
wrong: With a big army and lots of money
By hiring the best builders around
question.why: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.” The Lord’s Spirit would carry the work through.

bonus.q: In Zechariah 4:10, what kind of day should no one look down on?
bonus.hunt: In Zechariah 4, what kind of day should no one look down on?
bonus.why: Verse 10: “For who hath despised the day of small things?” A small start, like a temple’s first stones, is part of the Lord’s work.

image.alt: Etching of a tall seven-branched lampstand with a bowl on top and two olive trees dripping oil into it, as an angel shows it to the prophet Zechariah
image.credit: The Lampstand Seen in a Vision by Zechariah, by Jan Luyken, 1683. Public domain

reels.hook: Take one step toward God, and He comes toward you.
reels.body: Zechariah’s first message reminded the people of their fathers, who didn’t listen to the prophets and lost their land (Zechariah 1:4–6). Then came the Lord’s promise: “Turn ye unto me … and I will turn unto you.” In the Old Testament, turning to God means repenting. And it goes both ways. As we turn toward Him, He turns toward us. We never come back to Him alone.

verse.text: Therefore say thou unto them, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will turn unto you, saith the LORD of hosts.

question.q: What does the Lord promise when His people turn to Him?
question.right: He will turn to them too
wrong: He will give them a new king
He will make them rich again
question.why: “Turn ye unto me … and I will turn unto you.” Repenting isn’t a one-way trip. The Lord comes toward us as we come toward Him.

bonus.q: In Zechariah 1:4, what did the earlier prophets tell the fathers to turn from?
bonus.hunt: In Zechariah 1, what did the earlier prophets tell the fathers to turn from?
bonus.right: Their evil ways and evil doings
wrong: The idols of Egypt and Babylon
bonus.why: Verse 4: “Turn ye now from your evil ways, and from your evil doings: but they did not hear.” Their children could choose differently.
bonus.find: Turn ye now from your evil ways

image.alt: Painting of a father hugging his ragged, barefoot son on a path through golden fields as the son comes home
image.credit: The Prodigal Son, by Clark Kelley Price

reels.hook: Dirty clothes off, clean clothes on.
reels.body: In a vision, Zechariah saw Joshua the high priest standing before an angel in “filthy garments” (Zechariah 3:3), while Satan stood by to accuse him. The angel had the dirty clothes taken off and gave Joshua clean ones. Dirty clothes are like sins. Through Jesus Christ, our sins can be taken away too. We promise to follow Him when we’re baptized, and the sacrament helps us stay clean.

verse.text: And he answered and spake unto those that stood before him, saying, Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment.

question.q: In Zechariah’s vision, what did the clean clothes show?
wrong: Joshua was going to be king
Joshua had won a great battle
question.why: “I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment.” Iniquity means sin.

bonus.q: In Zechariah 3:2, what does the Lord call Joshua?
bonus.hunt: In Zechariah 3, what does the Lord call Joshua?
bonus.right: A burning stick pulled from the fire
wrong: A lamb saved from the hungry wolves
A fish pulled up out of the deep sea
bonus.why: Verse 2: “is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?” A brand is a burning stick. The Lord had rescued Joshua and his people.
bonus.find: a brand plucked out of the fire

image.alt: A man dressed in white raises his right arm as he baptizes a young boy, also in white, in the blue water of a baptismal font
image.credit: Boy Being Baptized, from the Church Media Library

reels.hook: Holy words, even on a horse’s bells.
reels.body: Zechariah saw a day when even ordinary things, like the bells on horses and the cooking pots, would say “HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD.” Today the words Holiness to the Lord are written on every temple. But Zechariah saw them on everyday things too. Holiness isn’t only for the temple. It’s for your whole life: how you talk, what you watch, how you treat your family.

verse.text: In that day shall there be upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD; and the pots in the LORD's house shall be like the bowls before the altar.

question.q: Why would ordinary pots and bells say “HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD”?
question.right: Even everyday things would be holy
wrong: They were made from temple gold
Only priests were allowed to use them
question.why: Zechariah saw that “the pots in the LORD's house shall be like the bowls before the altar.” In that day everything would be holy, not just the temple.

bonus.q: The lesson points to Exodus 28:36. What was HOLINESS TO THE LORD engraved on there?
bonus.hunt: The lesson points to Exodus 28. What was HOLINESS TO THE LORD engraved on there?
bonus.why: Exodus 28:36: “thou shalt make a plate of pure gold, and grave upon it … HOLINESS TO THE LORD.” The high priest wore it on his forehead (verse 38).
bonus.find: make a plate of pure gold

image.alt: The white Manila Philippines Temple with its tall spires at sunset, framed by palm trees
image.credit: Manila Philippines Temple in the Evening, from the Church Media Library

reels.hook: A King who rides a donkey, not a war horse.
reels.body: Zechariah saw a King coming to Jerusalem, “lowly, and riding upon an ass,” a donkey. Horses meant war, but kings also rode donkeys. More than 500 years later, Jesus rode a young donkey into Jerusalem, and crowds spread branches and shouted Hosanna (Matthew 21:8–9). That was Palm Sunday, the week before Easter. Matthew says it happened to fulfill this very prophecy (Matthew 21:4–5).

verse.text: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.

question.right: He rode into Jerusalem on a donkey
wrong: He was born in a stable in Bethlehem
He walked on the water to His friends
question.why: Zechariah saw the King “riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.” Jesus did just that on Palm Sunday (Matthew 21:7).

bonus.q: In Zechariah 9:16, what will the Lord’s people be like on His land?
bonus.hunt: In Zechariah 9, what will the Lord’s people be like on His land?
bonus.why: Verse 16: “they shall be as the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon his land.” Like jewels, His people shine for all to see.
bonus.find: they shall be as the stones of a crown

image.alt: Painting of Jesus Christ riding a white donkey through a stone archway into Jerusalem as people wave palm branches and spread cloth on the road
image.credit: Triumphal Entry (Christ’s Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem), by Harry Anderson

reels.hook: A shepherd paid the price of a slave.
reels.body: In Zechariah 11, the Lord had Zechariah act out a story. He worked as a shepherd for a flock, but the people didn’t want him. When he asked for his pay, they gave him “thirty pieces of silver,” the price of a slave. The Lord told him to throw it “to the potter in the house of the LORD” (Zechariah 11:13). Judas later sold Jesus for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15).

verse.text: And I said unto them, If ye think good, give me my price; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver.

question.q: What price did the people put on their shepherd?
question.why: “So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver.” It was a tiny price. Judas sold the Good Shepherd, Jesus, for the same amount.

bonus.q: In Zechariah 11:7, what did Zechariah name his two shepherd’s staffs?
bonus.hunt: In Zechariah 11, what did Zechariah name his two shepherd’s staffs?
bonus.why: Verse 7: “the one I called Beauty, and the other I called Bands.” Breaking them showed a broken covenant (verses 10 and 14).
bonus.find: the one I called Beauty, and the other I called Bands

image.alt: Painting of Jesus Christ as a shepherd, carrying a lamb in His arms while His flock of sheep walks beside Him
image.credit: The Good Shepherd, by Bernhard Plockhorst. Public domain

reels.hook: One day they’ll see the One they hurt, and cry.
reels.body: Zechariah saw a day when the people of Jerusalem “shall look upon me whom they have pierced,” and weep as if they had lost an only son. The Apostle John says this was about Jesus, whose side a soldier pierced with a spear on the cross (John 19:34–37). When Jesus comes again, many who did not know Him will finally see that He is their Messiah.

verse.text: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn.

question.q: Who is the One “whom they have pierced”?
question.why: John quotes these words about Jesus on the cross: “They shall look on him whom they pierced” (John 19:37).

bonus.q: In Zechariah 12:8, who will the weakest people in Jerusalem be like?
bonus.hunt: In Zechariah 12, who will the weakest people in Jerusalem be like?
bonus.why: Verse 8: “he that is feeble among them at that day shall be as David.” The Lord will make even the weakest strong.
bonus.find: he that is feeble among them at that day shall be as David

image.alt: Painting of Jesus Christ in a white robe and red sash coming down through the clouds with His arms open, as angels on each side blow trumpets
image.credit: The Second Coming, by Harry Anderson

reels.hook: He kept the marks in His hands so we’d know Him.
reels.body: Zechariah heard someone ask the Lord, “What are these wounds in thine hands?” He answers that He was wounded “in the house of my friends.” In Doctrine and Covenants 45:51–52 the Lord explains more: when He comes again, He will show the wounds in His hands and feet and say, “I am Jesus that was crucified” (Doctrine and Covenants 45:52). His wounds show how much He loves us.

verse.text: And one shall say unto him, What are these wounds in thine hands? Then he shall answer, Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends.

question.q: When Jesus comes again, what will help people know who He is?
question.right: The wounds in His hands and feet
wrong: A golden crown on His head
A sign written across the sky
question.why: He will show His wounds and say, “I am Jesus that was crucified” (Doctrine and Covenants 45:52).

bonus.q: In Zechariah 13:1, what will be opened for sin and uncleanness?
bonus.hunt: In Zechariah 13, what will be opened for sin and uncleanness?
bonus.why: Verse 1: “In that day there shall be a fountain opened … for sin and for uncleanness.” The Savior is the source that makes us clean.
bonus.find: there shall be a fountain opened

image.alt: Painting of the resurrected Jesus Christ holding out His hands to show the nail wounds to His disciples
image.credit: Jesus Shows His Wounds (Behold My Hands and Feet), by Harry Anderson

reels.hook: A mountain splits in two when He comes back.
reels.body: Zechariah saw the last days, when armies from many nations will fight against Jerusalem. Then shall “the LORD go forth, and fight against those nations” (Zechariah 14:3). His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, and the mountain will split in two, opening a valley for His people to escape. It’s the same mountain Jesus went up from to heaven (Acts 1:9–12).

verse.text: And his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east, and the mount of Olives shall cleave in the midst thereof toward the east and toward the west, and there shall be a very great valley; and half of the mountain shall remove toward the north, and half of it toward the south.

question.q: Where will the Lord’s feet stand in that day?
wrong: On the roof of the temple
question.why: “His feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives.” The mountain will split, making a valley for His people to flee through (verse 5).

bonus.q: In Zechariah 14:7, what will happen at evening time?
bonus.hunt: In Zechariah 14, what will happen at evening time?
wrong: It will be dark and cold
bonus.why: Verse 7: “at evening time it shall be light.” That day will not be like any other day.
bonus.find: at evening time it shall be light

image.alt: Photo of the green Mount of Olives seen through a stone archway on the Temple Mount, with the golden domes of a church on its slope
image.credit: The Mount of Olives from the Temple Mount, Jerusalem, photo by Beko, CC BY-SA 4.0

lines: In 520 BC the Lord sends Haggai to Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest. The people say it isn’t time yet to build the Lord’s house. (verses 1–2)
They live in fine paneled houses while the temple lies in ruins. The Lord tells them to consider their ways: they work hard but never have enough. (verses 3–7)
He tells them to bring wood and build. Because they left His house in ruins, He has held back the rain and their crops. (verses 8–11)
The leaders and the people obey and fear the Lord. He promises to be with them and stirs up their spirits, and they go to work on the temple. (verses 12–15)

review.about: “In 520 BC” comes from the Scripture Helps (“His prophecies are dated to 520 BC”); the verse dates it by Darius’s second year.
“Fine paneled houses” is for “ceiled houses” (paneled, as the BSB has it).

lines: Some remember Solomon’s temple and think the new one is nothing beside it. The Lord tells everyone to be strong and work, because He is with them. (verses 1–5)
He will shake the nations, and the Desire of All Nations, Jesus Christ, will come. This house will have greater glory, and there He will give peace. (verses 6–9)
Haggai teaches that touching holy things can’t make unclean people holy. But from the day the temple’s foundation is laid, the Lord will bless them. (verses 10–19)
The Lord will overthrow kingdoms and make Zerubbabel like His signet ring, a sign that He has chosen him. (verses 20–23)

review.about: “Jesus Christ” comes from the chapter heading (“Haggai speaks about the Messiah”) and the Scripture Helps, which say the title can refer to the Savior.

lines: Zechariah calls Judah to repent: if they turn to the Lord, He will turn to them. Their fathers didn’t listen to the prophets, and the Lord’s words came true. (verses 1–6)
In a night vision, riders on horses report that the whole earth is at rest. An angel asks how long Jerusalem must wait for mercy. (verses 7–12)
The Lord answers with comforting words. He has returned to Jerusalem with mercy, and His house and the cities of Judah will be built again. (verses 13–17)
Four horns that scattered Judah will be thrown down by four craftsmen the Lord sends. (verses 18–21)

review.about: “Craftsmen” is for the KJV’s “carpenters” (the Bible Dictionary uses “craftsmen” too).

lines: A man goes to measure Jerusalem, but it will be too full of people for walls. The Lord will be a wall of fire around it and its glory inside. (verses 1–5)
In the last days the Lord calls His scattered people to flee from the land of the north and come home. Whoever harms them harms what He holds most dear. (verses 6–9)
Zion can sing for joy: the Lord will come and live among His people. Many nations will join Him, and He will choose Jerusalem again. (verses 10–13)

review.about: “What He holds most dear” is for “the apple of his eye,” kept out of the card because APPLE is Tuesday’s Verse Word.

lines: In a vision, Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the Lord in filthy clothes, with Satan beside him to accuse him. The Lord rebukes Satan. (verses 1–3)
The dirty clothes are taken off, and Joshua gets clean clothes and a clean priest’s cap. His sins are taken away. (verses 4–5)
If Joshua walks in the Lord’s ways and keeps His commands, he will take care of the Lord’s house. (verses 6–7)
The Lord will bring His servant the Branch, the Messiah. At the Second Coming He will remove the land’s sin in one day. (verses 8–10)
An angel wakes Zechariah and shows him a golden lampstand with seven lamps, and two olive trees beside it. (verses 1–5)
The message to Zerubbabel: the work will be done not by might or power, but by the Lord’s Spirit. The mountain in front of him will become flat ground. (verses 6–7)
Zerubbabel laid the temple’s foundation, and his own hands will finish it. (verses 8–10)
The two olive trees are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth. (verses 11–14)
Some people send men to ask the priests whether they should keep fasting to mourn the temple’s fall. (verses 1–3)
The Lord asks if their fasts and feasts were really for Him, or only for themselves. He wanted them to listen to His prophets. (verses 4–7)
He calls them to judge fairly, show mercy and kindness, and never mistreat widows, orphans, strangers or the poor. (verses 8–10)
Their fathers hardened their hearts and wouldn’t listen, so the Lord scattered them and the land was left empty. (verses 11–14)
The Lord will return to Zion and live in Jerusalem. Old people and children playing will fill its streets again. (verses 1–5)
In the last days He will gather His people from east and west, and they will be His people. He tells them to be strong and build the temple. (verses 6–13)
He will bless them more than ever before. They must speak the truth, judge fairly and love peace. Their sad fasts will become happy feasts. (verses 14–19)
People from many nations will come to Jerusalem to seek the Lord, because they have heard that God is with His people. (verses 20–23)
Judgment will come on the proud cities around Israel, like Tyrus and Gaza, but the Lord will guard His house. (verses 1–8)
Zion can rejoice: her King, the Messiah, will come bringing salvation, humble and riding on a donkey. He will speak peace to the nations. (verses 9–10)
Because of His covenant, He will free prisoners from a pit with no water. (verses 11–12)
The Lord will make Judah and Ephraim His bow and arrows. He will defend them and save them like a shepherd saves his flock. (verses 13–17)

review.about: The heading says “Zechariah speaks as the Messiah”; the line names the King as the Messiah, as the heading does.

lines: Ask the Lord for rain, not idols, which only tell lies. Without a true shepherd, the people wander like lost sheep. (verses 1–2)
The Lord is angry with the bad shepherds. He will make Judah strong and save the house of Joseph, because He has mercy on them. (verses 3–7)
He has scattered them in far countries, but He will whistle for them, gather them and redeem them. They will remember Him and come home. (verses 8–12)

review.about: “Whistle” is for the KJV’s “hiss” (the heading says “hiss for them”); it means calling them, like a shepherd.

lines: The cedars of Lebanon and the oaks of Bashan fall, and the shepherds cry out. (verses 1–3)
The Lord has Zechariah act as shepherd of a flock headed for slaughter. He breaks one of his two staffs to show the covenant is broken. (verses 4–11)
He is paid thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave, and throws it to the potter in the Lord’s house. This points to the Messiah’s betrayal. (verses 12–14)

insights.title: Repentance is realignment
insights.text: “Consider your ways,” the Lord said, twice (verses 5 and 7). Dr. Anthony Sweat, a BYU religion professor, says this isn’t a scolding. He calls repentance realignment: noticing where we’ve drifted from God and steering back to Him. He says the invitation is hopeful and loving. The people of Haggai’s day took it that way. Instead of fighting the prophet, they went to work.

paras: Dr. Anthony Sweat breaks Haggai’s short book into four messages given over four months, which he names accusation, expectation, invitation and celebration. The first, all of chapter 1, names the problem. The people had come home from Babylon fifteen or sixteen years before, built themselves comfortable paneled houses, and kept saying it wasn’t yet time to build the Lord’s house (verses 2–4).

Twice the Lord says, “Consider your ways” (verses 5 and 7). Dr. Sweat doesn’t hear a condemnation in it. “The concept of repentance is constant reevaluation and constant realignment,” he says. We all drift, and our work is to compare our ways with the Lord’s and line back up. He calls the invitation “hopeful and it’s a loving thing.”

John Bytheway recalls President J. Reuben Clark’s picture of a mariner who, after fog and clouds, takes the first clear sky to find the stars, learn where he is and reset his course. Hank Smith adds that followHIM is a shame-free zone: the Atonement is a gift, not a guilt trip. Their models are Zerubbabel, Joshua and the people, who “obeyed the voice of the LORD” (Haggai 1:12) and within weeks were at work on the temple (verse 14).

insights.title: Zechariah in Doctrine and Covenants 45
insights.text: In 1831 the Lord gave Joseph Smith a revelation about His Second Coming, now Doctrine and Covenants 45. Scripture Central notes that, without naming Zechariah, it uses three of his prophecies: the Mount of Olives splitting (Zechariah 14:4), the question about His wounds (Zechariah 13:6), and the mourning for the One they pierced (Zechariah 12:10).

source.title: Why Does Doctrine and Covenants 45 Quote the Book of Zechariah?

insights.find: One additional Old Testament prophet cited—but not named—in this revelation is Zechariah.

paras: Doctrine and Covenants 45 came about March 7, 1831, while Joseph Smith was working on his inspired revision of the Bible. Much of it is the Lord’s own commentary on His Olivet Discourse in Matthew 24, given on the Mount of Olives. Steven C. Harper calls section 45 “the only source on earth in which the Savior of the world interprets and applies his own Olivet discourse.”

Besides Joel and Daniel, the Lord draws on Zechariah 12–14. Doctrine and Covenants 45:48 echoes the Mount of Olives splitting in two (Zechariah 14:4). Doctrine and Covenants 45:51–52 takes up the question, “What are these wounds in thine hands?” (Zechariah 13:6). And Doctrine and Covenants 45:53 echoes the mourning for the One “whom they have pierced.” In Zechariah 13 the words first described a false prophet; the Lord applies them to Himself, the One wrongly taken for one.

The KnoWhy links this verse to John 19:37, which applies it to the wounds Jesus received on the cross. When Israel at last recognizes Him, Stephen E. Robinson and H. Dean Garrett write, it will begin a great repentance, not for His death, since these Jews are not guilty of that, but “the same repentance that all who come unto Christ must go through.”

Why give such a revelation then? Joseph noted that false reports and lies were spreading to keep people from looking into the Church. Section 45 came to cheer the Saints, who, like Zechariah’s people, were trying to build temples and Zion. The promise in both is the same: the Lord remembers His covenant and will rescue His people.
