Then Haggai, the Lord’s messenger, gave the people the Lord’s message: “I am with you,” says the Lord.

So the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua, the son of Josedech, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people. They came and worked on the house of the Lord of Hosts, their God.
This was on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius.

review.about: “(of Persia)” is added to say who Darius was. The KJV spells the high priest’s father Josedech; the Hebrew and the BSB have Jehozadak. The plain words keep the KJV spelling here and in verses 12 and 14.
The KJV’s “ceiled houses” are houses with wood paneling on the walls and ceilings, a sign of wealth; the plain words say “paneled houses,” as the BSB does. No note.
The Hebrew word the KJV reads “over you” can also mean ‘because of you’ (BSB ‘on account of you’). The plain words follow the KJV.
This verse finishes verse 14 in the Hebrew (they started work on this day). The plain words add “This was” so it stands as its own line.

verses: On the twenty-first day of the seventh month, the word of the Lord came through Haggai the prophet. It said:
Speak now to Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua, the son of Josedech, the high priest, and to the rest of the people. Say to them:
Who is left among you who saw this house in its first glory? And how does it look to you now? Doesn’t it seem like nothing to you compared with that?

But now be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord. Be strong, Joshua, son of Josedech, the high priest. Be strong, all you people of the land, says the Lord, and work, for I am with you, says the Lord of Hosts.
Just as I promised in the covenant I made with you when you came out of Egypt, my Spirit stays among you. Don’t be afraid.
For this is what the Lord of Hosts says: Once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land.
I will shake all nations, and the desire of all nations will come. And I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord of Hosts.
The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, says the Lord of Hosts.
The glory of this latter house will be greater than the glory of the former house, says the Lord of Hosts. And in this place I will give peace, says the Lord of Hosts.
On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Haggai the prophet. It said:
This is what the Lord of Hosts says: Ask the priests what the law says. Ask them:
If someone carries holy meat from a sacrifice in the fold of his robe, and that fold touches bread, or stew, or wine, or oil, or any food, does that food become holy? The priests answered, “No.”
Then Haggai said, “If someone who is unclean from touching a dead body touches any of these, does it become unclean?” The priests answered, “It becomes unclean.”
Then Haggai answered: That is how this people is, and how this nation is in front of me, says the Lord. That is how all the work of their hands is, and whatever they offer there is unclean.
And now, please think carefully, from this day on, about the time before one stone was laid on another in the temple of the Lord.

Back then, when someone came to a pile of grain that should have been twenty measures, there were only ten. When someone came to the wine vat to draw out fifty measures from the press, there were only twenty.
I struck you with blight, mildew, and hail in all the work of your hands, yet you did not turn to me, says the Lord.
Think carefully, from this day on—from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, the day the foundation of the Lord’s temple was laid. Think about it:
Is there still seed in the barn? The vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree have not yet given their fruit. But from this day on I will bless you.
The word of the Lord came to Haggai a second time, on the twenty-fourth day of the month. It said:
Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, and say: I will shake the heavens and the earth.

I will overturn the thrones of kingdoms and destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the nations. I will overturn the chariots and those who ride in them. The horses and their riders will fall, each one by his brother’s sword.

On that day, says the Lord of Hosts, I will take you, Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel, says the Lord, and I will make you like a signet ring (the ring a king used to stamp his seal), for I have chosen you, says the Lord of Hosts.

notes.text: Hebrews quotes this promise: “Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven” (Hebrews 12:26). It says the shaking removes what can be shaken, and we receive “a kingdom which cannot be moved” (Hebrews 12:27–28).
The KJV says “the desire of all nations shall come.” The Hebrew word means something precious or longed for, and the BSB reads it as the nations’ riches: ‘they will come with all their treasures.’

review.about: A choice between readings. The KJV’s “the desire of all nations shall come” is often taught as the Savior; the BSB reads the same words as the nations’ treasures coming in (compare verse 8). The plain words keep the KJV’s wording, which leaves both open, with a note giving the BSB.

Hard Hebrew: the verse begins with no verb (‘the word that I cut with you’). The plain words follow the KJV’s “According to the word that I covenanted with you” as “Just as I promised in the covenant I made with you.” “My spirit” is given as “my Spirit,” as in the approved Isaiah chapters.

The KJV’s “from this day and upward” is unclear in the Hebrew too; it can look forward or back. The plain words say “from this day on,” as the BSB does, and make the rest of the verse the time they are to think about (verses 15–17 describe the hard years before the temple’s foundation).
“Holy flesh” is given as “holy meat from a sacrifice,” and the “skirt” of a garment as the fold of a robe. Verse 11’s “concerning the law” is given as “what the law says.”
A few words are added to say what a signet ring is. The KJV has “a signet”; the BSB ‘My signet ring.’

verses: In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to the prophet Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo. It said:
The Lord has been very angry with your fathers.
So say to them, This is what the Lord of Hosts says: Turn back to me, says the Lord of Hosts, and I will turn back to you, says the Lord of Hosts.

Don’t be like your fathers, to whom the earlier prophets called out, “This is what the Lord of Hosts says: Turn away now from your evil ways and your evil deeds.” But they would not listen or pay attention to me, says the Lord.
Your fathers—where are they now? And the prophets—do they live forever?

But my words and my laws, which I commanded my servants the prophets, didn’t they catch up with your fathers? Then they repented and said, “The Lord of Hosts has done to us just what He planned to do, as our ways and our deeds deserved.”
On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, the month Sebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to the prophet Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo:
I saw in the night, and look—a man riding on a red horse! He was standing among the myrtle trees in the hollow, and behind him were red, speckled, and white horses.
I asked, “What are these, my lord?” And the angel who was talking with me said to me, “I will show you what they are.”
Then the man standing among the myrtle trees answered, “These are the ones the Lord has sent to go back and forth through the earth.”
And they answered the angel of the Lord, who was standing among the myrtle trees, “We have gone back and forth through the earth, and look, the whole earth sits still and is at rest.”
Then the angel of the Lord said, “O Lord of Hosts, how long will you hold back your mercy from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which you have been angry with these seventy years?”
And the Lord answered the angel who was talking with me with kind words, words of comfort.
So the angel who was talking with me said to me, Call out this message: This is what the Lord of Hosts says: I am jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy.
And I am very angry with the nations that feel safe and at ease. For I was only a little angry, but they helped make the disaster worse.
So this is what the Lord says: I have come back to Jerusalem with mercy. My house will be built in it, says the Lord of Hosts, and a measuring line will be stretched out over Jerusalem.
Call out again: This is what the Lord of Hosts says: My cities will again overflow with good things, and the Lord will again comfort Zion and will again choose Jerusalem.
Then I looked up, and I saw four horns.
I asked the angel who was talking with me, “What are these?” He answered me, “These are the horns that have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem.”
Then the Lord showed me four craftsmen.

I asked, “What are these coming to do?” He said, “These are the horns that scattered Judah, so that no one could lift up his head. But these craftsmen have come to terrify them and to throw down the horns of the Gentiles, who lifted up their horn against the land of Judah to scatter it.”

notes.text: The KJV says “four carpenters.” The Hebrew word means skilled workmen in wood, stone or metal, and the BSB has ‘four craftsmen.’

review.about: Numbering: in Hebrew Bibles, verses 18–21 are chapter 2:1–4 (and the KJV’s 2:1–13 are the Hebrew 2:5–17). The plain words follow the KJV’s numbering, as the Hebrew and BSB lines in the app do. Horns are a picture of strength; verse 19 says whose.
The KJV’s “the son of Iddo the prophet” could make Iddo the prophet; the Hebrew and BSB make it Zechariah, and the plain words follow them, here and in verse 7.
“Jealous” is kept, as in the KJV: the Hebrew means a burning, protective love for Jerusalem. The message runs through verse 17, so it has no quote marks, as in the approved Jeremiah chapters.
The KJV’s “helped forward the affliction” means the nations made Judah’s punishment worse than the Lord intended. The plain words don’t name who He was angry with, as the KJV and Hebrew don’t.

verses: I looked up again, and I saw a man with a measuring line in his hand.
I asked, “Where are you going?” He said to me, “To measure Jerusalem, to see how wide it is and how long it is.”
Then the angel who was talking with me went out, and another angel came out to meet him.
He said to him, Run and tell this young man: Jerusalem will be lived in like towns without walls, because there will be so many people and animals in it.
For I will be a wall of fire all around her, says the Lord, and I will be the glory inside her.
Come! Come out and run away from the land of the north, says the Lord, for I have spread you out like the four winds of the sky, says the Lord.
Escape, Zion, you who live with the daughter of Babylon (the people of Babylon)!
For this is what the Lord of Hosts says: After the glory, He has sent me to the nations that robbed you—for whoever touches you touches the apple of His eye.
For look, I will shake my hand over them, and they will be robbed by those who served them. Then you will know that the Lord of Hosts has sent me.
Sing and be glad, daughter of Zion! For look, I am coming, and I will live among you, says the Lord.
Many nations will join themselves to the Lord on that day and will become my people. I will live among you, and you will know that the Lord of Hosts has sent me to you.
The Lord will take Judah as His own share in the holy land, and He will choose Jerusalem again.
Be silent before the Lord, all people, for He has risen up from His holy home.

review.about: Hard Hebrew. The KJV’s “After the glory hath he sent me” is kept word for word (“After the glory, He has sent me”); the BSB reads ‘After His Glory has sent Me,’ as a title for the Lord. “The apple of his eye” is literally the pupil; His is capitalized for the Lord, as in the BSB. No note; decide if one is wanted.
The KJV’s “Ho, ho” is a Hebrew call to get someone moving; the plain words say “Come! Come out,” and the BSB ‘Get up! Get up!’

The speaker in verses 8–11 is the Lord, who also says the Lord of Hosts has sent him. The plain words keep “me” and “my” lowercase, as for the Lord speaking everywhere in the approved chapters; the BSB capitalizes ‘Me.’
The message runs into verse 5, so it has no quote marks. “The daughter of Babylon” in verse 7 has a few words added to say who she is.

verses: Then he showed me Joshua the high priest standing in front of the angel of the Lord, and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him.
The Lord said to Satan, “May the Lord rebuke you, Satan! May the Lord, who has chosen Jerusalem, rebuke you! Isn’t this man a burning stick pulled out of the fire?”
Now Joshua was dressed in filthy clothes as he stood in front of the angel.
The angel said to those standing in front of him, “Take the filthy clothes off him.” And to Joshua he said, “Look, I have taken your sin away from you, and I will dress you in fine new clothes.”
Then I said, “Let them put a clean turban on his head.” So they put a clean turban on his head and dressed him in clothes, while the angel of the Lord stood by.
Then the angel of the Lord gave Joshua this solemn charge:

This is what the Lord of Hosts says: If you will walk in my ways and keep my charge, then you will also rule my house and take care of my courts, and I will give you a place to walk among these who are standing here.
Listen now, Joshua the high priest, you and your friends who sit in front of you, for they are men who are a sign. For look, I will bring my servant, the Branch.

For look at the stone I have set in front of Joshua. On this one stone are seven eyes. Look, I will carve its inscription, says the Lord of Hosts, and I will take away the sin of that land in one day.
On that day, says the Lord of Hosts, each of you will invite his neighbor to come and sit under the vine and under the fig tree.

notes.text: The KJV says Satan stood “to resist him.” The Hebrew verb is the root of the name Satan, which means ‘the accuser’ or ‘the adversary,’ and the BSB has ‘to accuse him.’

review.about: The plain words follow the Hebrew and BSB (“to accuse him”) over the KJV’s “to resist him,” with a note. The Hebrew says “the satan” (the accuser); the plain words keep the KJV’s name Satan.
“He” is given as “The angel” so it is clear who speaks (the BSB does the same). The KJV’s “change of raiment” is festival clothing, given as “fine new clothes.”

“Men wondered at” is, in Hebrew, ‘men of a sign’: Joshua and the priests with him stand for something to come. “The BRANCH,” in capitals in the KJV, is kept as a title, “the Branch”; Jeremiah 23:5 and Zechariah 6:12 use the same title for a coming King from David’s line. No note, since the New Testament does not quote it; decide if one is wanted.
The Hebrew says they will invite each other to “under a vine and under a fig tree,” a picture of peace (as in Micah 4:4). The plain words add “to come and sit.”

verses: Then the angel who was talking with me came back and woke me up, like someone who is woken from his sleep.
He asked me, “What do you see?” I said, “I see a lampstand made all of gold, with a bowl on top of it. It has seven lamps on it, and seven pipes going to the seven lamps on top of it.”
And there are two olive trees beside it, one on the right side of the bowl and the other on its left side.
Then I asked the angel who was talking with me, “What are these, my lord?”
The angel who was talking with me answered, “Don’t you know what these are?” I said, “No, my lord.”
So he said to me, This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the Lord of Hosts.
Who are you, great mountain? In front of Zerubbabel you will become flat ground. And he will bring out the top stone while people shout, “Grace, grace to it!”
The word of the Lord also came to me. It said:
The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house, and his hands will also finish it. Then you will know that the Lord of Hosts has sent me to you.

For who has looked down on the day of small things? They will rejoice when they see the plumb line (a weight on a string, for building straight walls) in Zerubbabel’s hand. These seven are the eyes of the Lord, which go back and forth through the whole earth.
Then I asked him, “What are these two olive trees on the right side and the left side of the lampstand?”
And I asked him again, “What are these two olive branches that pour out the golden oil through the two gold pipes?”
He answered me, “Don’t you know what these are?” I said, “No, my lord.”
So he said, “These are the two anointed ones who stand beside the Lord of the whole earth.”

notes.text: The KJV says “a candlestick all of gold.” It held oil lamps, not candles: the Hebrew word means a lampstand, as the BSB has it.

review.about: The Hebrew can be read as seven pipes for each lamp (‘seven and seven’); the plain words follow the KJV’s “seven pipes to the seven lamps,” and the BSB is close to it.

A few words are added to say what a plumb line (the KJV’s “plummet”) is. The KJV’s order is kept: they rejoice and see the plumb line, and the seven are the Lord’s eyes; the BSB makes the seven eyes the ones who rejoice.

The Hebrew for “the two anointed ones” is ‘the two sons of oil.’ Revelation 11:4 uses the picture of two olive trees for the two witnesses of the last days (D&C 77:15), but it reuses the words rather than saying who these two are, so there is no note (as decided for Isaiah 21:9).
“Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” is kept almost word for word, since it is well known. The message runs through verse 7, so it has no outer quote marks.

verses: In the fourth year of King Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, the month Chisleu.
The people of Bethel had sent Sherezer and Regem-melech and their men to pray to the Lord,
and to ask the priests of the house of the Lord of Hosts, and the prophets, “Should I weep and fast in the fifth month, setting myself apart as I have done for so many years?”
Then the word of the Lord of Hosts came to me. It said:
Say to all the people of the land and to the priests: When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month and the seventh month all these seventy years, did you really fast for me—for me?
And when you ate and when you drank, weren’t you eating and drinking just for yourselves?

Shouldn’t you have listened to the words the Lord called out through the earlier prophets, when Jerusalem was full of people and doing well, along with the cities around it, and when people lived in the south and in the lowlands?
And the word of the Lord came to Zechariah. It said:
This is what the Lord of Hosts says: Judge with true justice. Show mercy and compassion to each other.
Don’t mistreat widows, orphans, foreigners, or the poor. And don’t plan evil in your hearts against each other.
But they refused to listen. They stubbornly turned their shoulders away and covered their ears so they wouldn’t hear.
They made their hearts as hard as flint so they would not hear the law or the words the Lord of Hosts had sent by His Spirit through the earlier prophets. So great anger came from the Lord of Hosts.
So, just as He called and they would not listen, so they called and I would not listen, says the Lord of Hosts.

I scattered them with a whirlwind among all the nations they did not know. The land they left behind became so empty that no one came or went through it, because they turned the pleasant land into a wasteland.

notes.text: The KJV says they sent men “unto the house of God.” In Hebrew this is Beth-el, which means ‘house of God’ and is also the name of a town. The BSB reads ‘the people of Bethel had sent Sharezer.’

review.about: A choice between readings. The KJV reads Beth-el as the place they were sent to (“the house of God”); the BSB and most modern translations read it as the town that sent them. The plain words follow the Hebrew and BSB (the Hebrew verb “sent” is singular, fitting “Bethel” as the sender), with a note giving the KJV. Your call.

The KJV’s “separating myself” is a Hebrew word for setting oneself apart, here by fasting (BSB ‘weep and fast’). The plain words say both. The fifth-month fast mourned the burning of the temple (2 Kings 25:8–9); no note.
The KJV’s “the south and the plain” are the Negev and the Shephelah, the low hills west of Judah; the plain words say “the south and the lowlands.”
The Hebrew says “as he called” and then “I would not listen,” the Lord speaking of Himself both ways. The plain words capitalize He for the Lord; the BSB evens it to ‘I.’

verses: Again the word of the Lord of Hosts came to me. It said:
This is what the Lord of Hosts says: I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy. I am jealous for her with great fury.
This is what the Lord says: I have come back to Zion, and I will live in Jerusalem. Jerusalem will be called a city of truth, and the mountain of the Lord of Hosts will be called the holy mountain.
This is what the Lord of Hosts says: Old men and old women will again sit in the streets of Jerusalem, each with a walking stick in his hand because he is so old.
And the streets of the city will be full of boys and girls playing there.
This is what the Lord of Hosts says: If this seems too hard to the remnant of this people in those days, should it also seem too hard to me? says the Lord of Hosts.
This is what the Lord of Hosts says: Look, I will save my people from the land of the east and from the land of the west.
I will bring them back, and they will live in Jerusalem. They will be my people, and I will be their God, in truth and in righteousness.

This is what the Lord of Hosts says: Let your hands be strong, you who are hearing these words in these days from the mouths of the prophets, who were there on the day the foundation of the house of the Lord of Hosts was laid so the temple could be built.
For before those days there were no wages for people or for animals. There was no peace for anyone who went out or came in, because of the trouble, for I turned everyone against his neighbor.
But now I will not treat the remnant of this people as I did in the past, says the Lord of Hosts.

For the seed will grow well. The vine will give its fruit, the ground will give its crops, and the sky will give its dew. And I will give the remnant of this people all these things to have as their own.
House of Judah and house of Israel, just as you were a curse among the nations, so I will save you, and you will be a blessing. Don’t be afraid, but let your hands be strong.
For this is what the Lord of Hosts says: When your fathers made me angry, I planned to punish you, says the Lord of Hosts, and I did not hold back.
So now, in these days, I have planned again to do good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. Don’t be afraid.
These are the things you must do: Speak the truth to each other. In your city gates, where cases are judged, give judgments that are true and that bring peace.
Don’t plan evil in your hearts against your neighbor, and don’t love to swear false oaths. For I hate all these things, says the Lord.
And the word of the Lord of Hosts came to me. It said:

This is what the Lord of Hosts says: The fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth will become times of joy and gladness and happy feasts for the house of Judah. So love truth and peace.
This is what the Lord of Hosts says: Peoples will still come, people who live in many cities.
The people who live in one city will go to another and say, “Let’s go right away to pray to the Lord and to seek the Lord of Hosts. I’m going too!”
Yes, many peoples and strong nations will come to Jerusalem to seek the Lord of Hosts and to pray to the Lord.

This is what the Lord of Hosts says: In those days ten men from all the languages of the nations will take hold of the edge of a Jew’s robe and say, “Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.”

notes.text: The KJV says “I repented not.” The Hebrew word means to relent or change course, and the BSB has ‘I did not relent.’

review.about: The KJV puts this in the past (“I was jealous”); the Hebrew verb can be read as now, as the BSB does (‘I am jealous’). The plain words follow the Hebrew and BSB.
The KJV’s “marvellous” is a Hebrew word for something too hard or too wonderful, the same word as “Is any thing too hard for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14). The plain words say “too hard.”
The KJV’s “because of the affliction” can also be read ‘from the enemy’ (BSB). The plain words follow the KJV (“because of the trouble”).
Where the KJV says “I repented not,” the plain words say “I did not hold back,” with a note, as with “repent” in Jeremiah 18:8.
“Take hold” comes twice in the Hebrew (“shall take hold … even shall take hold of the skirt”); the plain words say it once. The “skirt” is the edge of the robe.

verses: The burden (a heavy message) of the word of the Lord is against the land of Hadrach, and Damascus is where it will rest, when the eyes of all people, and of all the tribes of Israel, will look to the Lord.
It is also against Hamath, which borders it, and against Tyrus and Zidon, even though they are very wise.
Tyrus built herself a fortress and piled up silver like dust and fine gold like the mud in the streets.
Look, the Lord will take away all she has. He will strike down her power on the sea, and she will be burned up with fire.

Ashkelon will see it and be afraid. Gaza will see it and be in great pain, and so will Ekron, for what she hoped in will put her to shame. The king will be gone from Gaza, and no one will live in Ashkelon.
A people of mixed birth will live in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines.

I will take the blood out of his mouth and the disgusting foods from between his teeth. Those who are left will belong to our God. They will be like a leader in Judah, and Ekron will be like a Jebusite.
I will camp around my house to guard it against the army, against those who pass through and those who return. No oppressor will march through them anymore, for now I have seen it with my own eyes.

Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Look, your King is coming to you. He is righteous and brings salvation. He is humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow used in battle will be cut off. He will speak peace to the nations. His rule will reach from sea to sea, and from the river (the Euphrates) to the ends of the earth.
As for you, because of the blood of your covenant, I have set your prisoners free from the pit that has no water.
Come back to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope! Even today I announce that I will give you back twice as much.
For I have bent Judah like my bow and filled it with Ephraim. I have stirred up your sons, Zion, against your sons, Greece, and made you like a mighty man’s sword.
Then the Lord will appear over them, and His arrow will flash out like lightning. The Lord God will blow the trumpet (a ram’s horn), and He will go out in the whirlwinds of the south.

The Lord of Hosts will defend them. They will devour, and they will conquer with sling stones. They will drink and roar as if from wine. They will be full like the bowls used at the altar, like the corners of the altar.
On that day the Lord their God will save them as the flock of His people. They will be like the jewels of a crown, lifted up like a flag over His land.
How great His goodness is, and how great His beauty! Grain will make the young men thrive, and new wine the young women.

notes.text: Matthew says this was fulfilled when Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey: “Behold, thy King cometh unto thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass” (Matthew 21:4–5).
The KJV’s “Greece” is Javan in the Hebrew, the name of a grandson of Noah: “The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan” (Genesis 10:2).
The KJV says “how great is his goodness, and how great is his beauty!” The BSB reads it of God’s people instead: ‘How lovely they will be, and how beautiful!’

review.about: He and His are capitalized for the King in verses 9–10, as the BSB does, because Matthew 21:4–5 says it is Jesus. The KJV’s “having salvation” is one Hebrew word that can mean ‘saved’ or ‘victorious’ (BSB); the plain words say “brings salvation.” Check that wording.
The KJV’s “a bastard” is a Hebrew word for someone of mixed or unlawful birth (BSB ‘a mixed race’). The plain words say “a people of mixed birth.” No note.

Verses 7 and 15 are hard. In verse 7 the Philistines stop eating blood and food offered to idols, and the survivors join Judah as the Jebusites of Jerusalem once did. The plain words keep the KJV’s “his” and “governor” (as “a leader”) and add nothing more.
The Hebrew and the KJV say “the blood of thy covenant”; the BSB has ‘My covenant.’ The plain words follow the Hebrew (“your covenant”).

Hard Hebrew. “Subdue with sling stones” may mean trampling the enemy’s sling stones underfoot. The bowls are the bowls of blood at the altar, and the altar’s corners were splashed with blood; the plain words say only “the bowls used at the altar.”

The KJV’s “his” is read as the Lord’s and capitalized; the BSB reads it as the people’s, so there is a note. “Cheerful” is a Hebrew word for growing strong (BSB ‘flourish’); the plain words say “thrive.”

verses: Ask the Lord for rain in the time of the latter rain (the spring rain). The Lord makes the storm clouds and gives people showers of rain, and green plants in the field for everyone.
For the idols speak nonsense, and the fortune-tellers see lies. They tell false dreams and give empty comfort. So the people wander like sheep. They are in trouble because there is no shepherd.

My anger burns against the shepherds, and I will punish the goats (the leaders). For the Lord of Hosts has come to care for His flock, the house of Judah, and He will make them like His splendid horse in battle.
From Judah will come the cornerstone, from him the tent peg, from him the battle bow, and from him every ruler together.
They will be like mighty men in battle, trampling their enemies in the mud of the streets. They will fight, because the Lord is with them, and the men riding horses will be put to shame.

I will make the house of Judah strong, and I will save the house of Joseph. I will bring them back and settle them, because I have mercy on them. They will be as if I had never cast them off, for I am the Lord their God, and I will hear them.
The people of Ephraim will be like a mighty man, and their hearts will be glad as if from wine. Their children will see it and be glad. Their hearts will rejoice in the Lord.
I will whistle for them and gather them, for I have redeemed them, and they will become as many as they were before.
I will scatter them like seed among the peoples, and in far countries they will remember me. They will live, along with their children, and they will come back.
I will bring them back from the land of Egypt and gather them from Assyria. I will bring them into the land of Gilead and Lebanon, until there is no room left for them.

He will pass through the sea of trouble and strike the waves in the sea, and all the depths of the river (the Nile) will dry up. The pride of Assyria will be brought down, and the scepter of Egypt will go away.
I will make them strong in the Lord, and they will walk up and down in His name, says the Lord.

notes.text: The KJV says “every oppressor.” The Hebrew word can mean a harsh master or a ruler, and the BSB reads ‘every ruler.’

review.about: The KJV has the past (“was kindled,” “I punished the goats”); the Hebrew and BSB read the punishment as coming. The plain words follow them. The “goats” are the leaders (BSB ‘leaders’), so a word is added in brackets. “Goodly horse” is a royal war horse.
“Out of him” is Judah (verse 3), named as the BSB does. The KJV’s “nail” is a tent peg, and its past tense (“came forth”) is given as future, as in the Hebrew and BSB.

Hard Hebrew: “he shall pass through the sea with affliction.” “He” may be the Lord leading His people, as at the Red Sea, or Israel (the BSB has ‘They’). The plain words keep a lowercase “he,” as the KJV does. “The river” is the Hebrew word for the Nile.
The KJV’s “idols” are teraphim, household idols used to ask about the future. The plain words keep “idols.”

verses: Open your doors, Lebanon, so the fire can burn up your cedars!
Wail, fir tree, for the cedar has fallen, because the mighty trees are ruined! Wail, you oaks of Bashan, for the thick forest has come down!
Listen to the shepherds wailing, for their glory is ruined! Listen to the young lions roaring, for the pride of the Jordan, its thick woods, is ruined!
This is what the Lord my God says: Feed the flock that is marked for slaughter.
Those who buy them kill them and feel no guilt. Those who sell them say, “Blessed be the Lord, for I am rich!” And their own shepherds have no pity on them.

For I will no longer have pity on the people who live in the land, says the Lord. Look, I will hand each person over to his neighbor and to his king. They will crush the land, and I will not rescue them from their hands.
So I fed the flock marked for slaughter, the poor of the flock. I took two staffs for myself. One I called Beauty (or Favor), and the other I called Bands (or Union). And I fed the flock.
In one month I cut off three shepherds. I lost patience with them, and they hated me too.
Then I said, “I will not feed you anymore. Let the dying die, and let what is to be destroyed be destroyed. And let those who are left eat each other’s flesh.”
Then I took my staff called Beauty and broke it in two, to break the covenant I had made with all the peoples.
It was broken that day. And so the poor of the flock who were watching me knew it was the word of the Lord.
I said to them, “If it seems right to you, pay me my price. If not, keep it.” So they weighed out my price: thirty pieces of silver.
Then the Lord said to me, “Throw it to the potter”—that fine price they valued me at! So I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them to the potter in the house of the Lord.
Then I broke my other staff, Bands, in two, to break the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.
Then the Lord said to me, “Take once more the things a foolish shepherd uses.”

For look, I will raise up a shepherd in the land who will not care for those that are perishing, or look for the young ones, or heal the injured, or feed the healthy. Instead he will eat the meat of the fat sheep and tear off their hooves.
How terrible for the worthless shepherd who leaves the flock! The sword will strike his arm and his right eye. His arm will wither away completely, and his right eye will go completely blind.

notes.text: Matthew says verses 12–13 were fulfilled when Judas threw back the money paid to betray Jesus, and the priests bought the potter’s field with it: “they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued” (Matthew 27:9–10).
The KJV says “the idol shepherd.” The Hebrew word means worthless and is often used for idols; the BSB has ‘the worthless shepherd.’

review.about: The KJV has “I will feed”; the Hebrew verb tells what the prophet did (BSB ‘So I pastured’), and the plain words follow the Hebrew. The staffs keep the KJV’s names, Beauty and Bands, with the Hebrew meanings Favor and Union (BSB) in brackets.

“A goodly price” is said with scorn: thirty pieces of silver was the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32). The plain words say “that fine price” and leave the scorn to the reader. Me is lowercase for the speaker, as everywhere.

The KJV’s “forest of the vintage” follows the written Hebrew; the Hebrew as read aloud has ‘the dense forest’ (BSB), and the plain words follow that. Verse 3’s “pride of Jordan” is the thick woods along the river, given as both.
The KJV states what will happen (“the sword shall be upon his arm”); the BSB makes it a curse (‘May a sword strike’). The plain words follow the KJV.

verses: The burden (a heavy message) of the word of the Lord for Israel, says the Lord, who stretches out the heavens, lays the foundation of the earth, and forms the spirit of man inside him:
Look, I will make Jerusalem a cup that makes all the peoples around it stagger, when they lay siege against Judah as well as against Jerusalem.
On that day I will make Jerusalem a heavy stone for all the peoples. Everyone who tries to lift it will be badly hurt, even though all the nations of the earth gather together against it.

On that day, says the Lord, I will strike every horse with panic and its rider with madness. I will keep my eyes open over the house of Judah, but I will strike every horse of the peoples with blindness.
Then the leaders of Judah will say in their hearts, “The people who live in Jerusalem are my strength in the Lord of Hosts, their God.”

On that day I will make the leaders of Judah like a pot of fire in a pile of wood, like a burning torch in a bundle of grain. They will devour all the peoples around them, on the right and on the left. And Jerusalem will be lived in again in her own place, in Jerusalem.
The Lord will also save the tents of Judah first, so that the glory of the house of David and the glory of the people of Jerusalem will not be greater than Judah’s.
On that day the Lord will defend the people of Jerusalem. The weakest among them on that day will be like David, and the house of David will be like God, like the angel of the Lord going before them.
On that day I will set out to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem.

I will pour out on the house of David and on the people of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of prayers for mercy. They will look on me, the one they pierced, and they will mourn for Him as someone mourns for an only son. They will grieve bitterly for Him, as someone grieves for a firstborn son.
On that day the mourning in Jerusalem will be great, like the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon.
The land will mourn, each family by itself: the family of the house of David by itself, and their wives by themselves; the family of the house of Nathan by itself, and their wives by themselves;
The family of the house of Levi by itself, and their wives by themselves; the family of Shimei by itself, and their wives by themselves;
And all the families that are left, each family by itself, and their wives by themselves.

notes.text: John says this scripture was fulfilled when a soldier pierced Jesus’ side on the cross: “They shall look on him whom they pierced” (John 19:37).

The Savior said that when He comes, “then shall the Jews look upon me” (D&C 45:51) and learn, “I am Jesus that was crucified” (D&C 45:52). “Then shall they lament because they persecuted their king” (D&C 45:53).

review.about: The Lord says “me, whom they have pierced,” then “mourn for him”: the Hebrew changes person, as the KJV does. “Me” stays lowercase like the Lord’s other words; “Him” is capitalized because John 19:37 and D&C 45:51–53 say He is Jesus (the BSB capitalizes both). “Supplications” is given as “prayers for mercy.”
Hadadrimmon and Megiddon keep the KJV spellings (BSB ‘Hadad-rimmon,’ ‘Megiddo’). What the mourning of Hadadrimmon was is not known for sure, so the plain words say no more than the KJV.

The KJV’s “hearth of fire among the wood” is a pot holding live coals (BSB ‘firepot’), given as “a pot of fire in a pile of wood.” “Governors” (here and in verse 5) is given as “leaders,” since the Hebrew word means clan chiefs.
Verses 12–14 are one sentence in the KJV, as here; each family and its wives mourn apart.

verses: On that day a fountain will be opened for the house of David and for the people of Jerusalem, to wash away sin and uncleanness.

On that day, says the Lord of Hosts, I will cut off the names of the idols from the land, and they will not be remembered anymore. I will also remove the false prophets and the unclean spirit from the land.

And if anyone still prophesies, his own father and mother will say to him, “You must not live, because you speak lies in the name of the Lord.” And his own father and mother will stab him when he prophesies.
On that day every prophet will be ashamed of his vision when he prophesies. They will not wear a rough, hairy coat to fool people.
Instead he will say, “I am not a prophet. I am a farmer, for someone bought me as a servant when I was young.”
And someone will ask him, “What are these wounds in your hands?” He will answer, “The wounds I was given in the house of my friends.”
Wake up, sword, against my shepherd, against the man who is my companion, says the Lord of Hosts. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered, and I will turn my hand on the little ones.
In the whole land, says the Lord, two parts out of three will be cut off and die, but the third part will be left in it.

And I will bring that third part through the fire. I will refine them as silver is refined and test them as gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, “They are my people,” and they will say, “The Lord is my God.”

notes.text: The KJV says “man taught me to keep cattle from my youth.” The BSB reads the Hebrew as ‘I was purchased as a servant in my youth.’

When the Savior comes again and the Jews ask, “What are these wounds in thine hands and in thy feet?” (D&C 45:51), He will answer, “These wounds are the wounds with which I was wounded in the house of my friends” (D&C 45:52).
On the night before He died, Jesus told His disciples they would all fall away, “for it is written, I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered abroad” (Matthew 26:31).

review.about: In the Hebrew the one asked follows on from the false prophet of verses 4–5, so the plain words keep “him” and “he” lowercase, as the KJV does, and the note gives D&C 45:51–52, where the Savior uses these words of Himself. “In your hands” follows the KJV and D&C; the Hebrew says ‘between your hands’ (BSB ‘on your chest’). Your call on the capitals.

“False” is added to “the prophets,” since verses 3–5 show who they are. Verse 3’s “thrust him through” (the law’s penalty for a false prophet, Deuteronomy 13:5–10) is given as “stab him,” no more plainly than the KJV.

The KJV reads the Hebrew as “man taught me to keep cattle”; the BSB and other modern translations as ‘a man bought me’ (made me his servant). The plain words follow the Hebrew and BSB, with a note giving the KJV.

Jesus applies this verse to Himself (Matthew 26:31, note), so the BSB writes ‘My Shepherd’ and ‘the Shepherd.’ The plain words keep the KJV’s lowercase, as with “king” in Isaiah 33:17. “I will turn mine hand upon the little ones” may mean against them or to care for them; the plain words keep “on.”

verses: Look, the day of the Lord is coming, when the loot taken from you will be divided up right inside your city.

For I will gather all nations against Jerusalem to fight. The city will be captured, the houses robbed, and the women abused. Half of the city will go away as captives, but the rest of the people will not be cut off from the city.
Then the Lord will go out and fight against those nations, as when He fought in the day of battle.

On that day His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, which faces Jerusalem on the east. The Mount of Olives will split in two from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.

And you will run away through the valley of the mountains, for the valley of the mountains will reach to Azal. Yes, you will run away just as you ran from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Then the Lord my God will come, and all the saints with you.
On that day the light will be neither bright nor dark.
It will be one special day, known to the Lord—not day and not night. But in the evening there will be light.
On that day living waters will flow out from Jerusalem, half of them toward the eastern sea (the Dead Sea) and half toward the western sea (the Mediterranean). It will be so in summer and in winter.
The Lord will be king over all the earth. On that day there will be one Lord, and His name will be one.

The whole land, from Geba to Rimmon south of Jerusalem, will be made flat like a plain. But Jerusalem will be lifted up and lived in, in her own place—from Benjamin’s gate to the place of the first gate, to the corner gate, and from the tower of Hananeel to the king’s winepresses.
People will live in it, and it will never again be completely destroyed. Jerusalem will be lived in safely.

This is the plague the Lord will strike all the peoples with who have fought against Jerusalem: their flesh will waste away while they are still standing on their feet, their eyes will waste away in their sockets, and their tongues will waste away in their mouths.
On that day a great panic from the Lord will come over them. Each one will grab his neighbor’s hand, and each will raise his hand against his neighbor.
Judah also will fight at Jerusalem. And the wealth of all the nations around will be gathered together—gold, silver, and clothing—in great amounts.
A plague like this one will also strike the horses, mules, camels, donkeys, and all the animals in those camps.

Then everyone who is left of all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up year after year to worship the King, the Lord of Hosts, and to keep the Feast of Tabernacles (the harvest festival of shelters).
And if any of the families of the earth will not come up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord of Hosts, they will have no rain.
If the family of Egypt, who have no rain, does not go up and come, there will be the plague the Lord uses to strike the nations that don’t come up to keep the Feast of Tabernacles.
This will be the punishment of Egypt, and the punishment of all nations that don’t come up to keep the Feast of Tabernacles.
On that day the words “Holiness to the Lord” will be on the bells of the horses. And the cooking pots in the Lord’s house will be like the bowls in front of the altar.

Yes, every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to the Lord of Hosts. All who offer sacrifices will come and take some of them and cook in them. And on that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the Lord of Hosts.

notes.text: The Lord told Joseph Smith this will happen when He comes again: “then shall the Lord set his foot upon this mount, and it shall cleave in twain” (D&C 45:48).
The KJV says “all the saints with thee,” as the Hebrew does. The BSB reads ‘all the holy ones with Him,’ as the ancient Greek translation does.
The KJV says “the light shall not be clear, nor dark.” The Hebrew here is hard to read, and the BSB has ‘there will be no light, no cold or frost.’

review.about: The KJV’s “the women ravished” is given as “the women abused,” which is true to the Hebrew without being more graphic than the KJV. Verse 12’s plague (“consume away”) is given as “waste away.” Both are hard for a child; decide if they read right.
Hard Hebrew (see the note). The plain words follow the KJV, as the approved chapters do where the Hebrew is unsure.

Hard Hebrew. The KJV reads “that have no rain” as describing Egypt, which is watered by the Nile, not by rain; the BSB reads ‘then the rain will not fall on them.’ The plain words follow the KJV. No note; decide if one is wanted.

“HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD” is given as “Holiness to the Lord,” the words on the high priest’s gold plate (Exodus 28:36) and on Latter-day Saint temples. A note was left out because the README’s note kinds don’t cover it; decide if one is wanted.

The Hebrew word for “Canaanite” can also mean a trader. The plain words keep “Canaanite,” as the KJV and BSB do. In verse 16 a few words say what the Feast of Tabernacles was; in verse 8 the eastern and western seas are named.

treasure.means: A signet ring or seal. Pressing it into clay or wax marked something as belonging to its owner.
treasure.more: The Lord called Zerubbabel His signet and said, “I have chosen thee.” He was close to the Lord and trusted to finish the Lord’s temple.

treasure.means: A sprout or new shoot growing up out of a plant. Here it is a title for the promised Messiah.
treasure.more: “The BRANCH” is a name for Jesus Christ, the new shoot growing from King David’s family tree, sent to bring God’s people new life.

treasure.means: A lampstand that held oil lamps, not candles. A golden one gave light inside the tabernacle and temple.
treasure.more: Zechariah saw a golden lampstand kept full of oil by two olive trees. Its message: the Lord’s work succeeds “not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.”

treasure.means: Poor, humble, lowly. Someone who doesn’t show off or push himself above other people.
treasure.more: The promised King would come humbly, riding a donkey. Jesus fulfilled this when He rode into Jerusalem on a donkey (Matthew 21:5).

treasure.means: To pierce: to stab right through something, like with a spear or a sword.
treasure.more: John saw this fulfilled when a soldier pierced Jesus’ side with a spear (John 19:34, 37). One day the Jews will see His wounds and know Him (D&C 45:51–52).

treasure.means: Holiness: being set apart for God, separate from what is ordinary or unclean.
treasure.more: Zechariah saw a day when even horse bells and cooking pots would be holy to the Lord. Our temples carry the same words: “Holiness to the Lord.”
